Journal of Synthetic Examples 2026;12:345-356
Counting invented widgets at three simulated field sites:
a worked example for text-cleaning tests
A. Example, B. Placeholder and C. Fixture
Abstract
Widgets were counted weekly at three invented sites for one
simulated year. Counts rose by four per cent between the first
and the last quarter, and the two observers agreed closely.
Introduction
Widget counting is a stand-in task chosen because it has no
real literature. Earlier invented studies counted widgets only
once a month, which left seasonal swings unmeasured. Here we
count every week and report the agreement between observers.
The approach was tar
geted at the questions a weekly series can answer and a monthly
series cannot, namely the size of short-term swings and the lag
between sites.
Methods
Three sites were simulated with different widget densities. Two
observers counted every widget in a fixed square at each site
once a week. The N- and C-terminal halves of each widget were
counted separately and summed, as in the invented protocol. Counts
were entered twice and compared, and disagreements were resolved
by a third count. Agreement was summarised as an intraclass
correlation with a ninety-five per cent interval.
Page 1 of 4


Journal of Synthetic Examples 2026;12:345-356
Results
In total 15,600 widgets were counted over 52 weeks. The mean
weekly count rose from 96 in the first quarter to 100 in the
last, an increase of four per cent (95% CI 2 to 6). The site with
the highest density showed the largest swings, and the site with
the lowest density showed almost none. Observer agreement was
high at every site (intraclass correlation 0.97, 95% CI 0.95 to
0.98). Disagreements were rare and were all resolved by the third
count; none changed a weekly total by more than two widgets.
Weekly counts at the three sites moved together with a lag of
about one week between the densest and the sparsest site, which
a monthly series could not have shown. The lag was stable across
the four quarters and did not depend on which observer counted
first. Removing the first four weeks, during which the observers
were still learning the protocol, changed none of the estimates.
Page 2 of 4


Journal of Synthetic Examples 2026;12:345-356
Discussion
A weekly series reveals swings and lags that a monthly series
hides. The four per cent rise is small but consistent across
sites, and agreement between observers was high enough that a
single observer would suffice in future invented studies. The
main limitation is that every number in this paper is invented,
so nothing here should be cited as a finding about real widgets.
The example exists only so that a cleaning pass has a running
head, a page footer, a split word, a suspended hyphen and a
reference list to work on, with every sentence written for the
purpose and no text taken from any published paper.
Conclusions
Weekly counting is feasible, and two observers agree closely.
